meta.blurb: Horses had vanished from North America for ten thousand years when the Spanish brought them back. Soon the Comanche, once a mountain people on foot, dominated the southern Plains from the saddle. Then came war, loss and survival.
meta.bible: Subject: the rise, power, fall and survival of the Comanche people of the southern Great Plains, with the horse and the Bison as the heart of the story. Dates are approximate and hedged; where historians disagree, the text says so. Numunu: the Comanche name for themselves, usually translated as the People. Comanche: a name from the Ute language, often translated as enemy. Comancheria: the Comanche homeland on the southern Plains, in what is now Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, New Mexico and Colorado. Shoshone: a related people of the mountains from whom the Comanche came. Great Plains: the huge grassland of North America. Spain, Spanish, Mexico, Texas, United States, Santa Fe, Taos, Pueblo, Apache, Lipan, Ute, Kiowa, Wichita, Taovayas, Comancheros. Bands: Penateka, Kotsoteka, Yamparika, Nokoni, Quahadi (names usually translated as Honey Eaters, Buffalo Eaters, Root Eaters, Wanderers and Antelopes). Terms: Tipi, Travois, Mustang, Sinew, Lance, Council. Key events: horses brought by Spain from 1493 and to New Mexico in 1598; the Pueblo Revolt of 1680; the Spanish peace made by Anza in 1786; the Council House Fight of March 1840 in San Antonio; the Great Raid and Plum Creek of August 1840; Medicine Lodge, 1867; Adobe Walls, June 1874; the Red River War of 1874 and 1875; Palo Duro Canyon, September 1874; the Quahadi surrender at Fort Sill in June 1875; Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 1903; Comanche code talkers of the Second World War. Places: Red River, Fort Sill, Oklahoma, Lawton, Palo Duro Canyon, Llano Estacado, San Antonio, Linnville, Plum Creek, Mackenzie. Numbers are hedged: some historians estimate perhaps 20,000 Comanche or more around 1800; a few hundred wild bison were left by about 1890; more than 15,000 enrolled Comanche citizens today. Violence on every side is told plainly and without gore. Voice and tone: respectful, clear and fair; the Comanche are people with a history, not a legend. No invented quotes, numbers or events.

B1B2: In the middle of North America lies the Great Plains, a vast grassland with few trees and a huge sky. For a very long time, this open land was home to millions of wild animals.
The animal at the centre of Plains life was the bison, often called the buffalo. Herds were so big that, in the 1800s, some travellers said it took hours for one to pass.
Before the horse came, people on the Plains travelled on foot. They used strong dogs to drag their belongings on a simple frame of poles called a travois.
Hunting bison on foot was dangerous, because the animals are fast and strong. People worked together to drive herds over cliffs or into traps, and then everyone shared the meat.

The story of the horse began in North America, where its earliest ancestors lived millions of years ago. About 10,000 years ago, horses disappeared from the continent, and for a long time no one rode here.
Horses returned across the sea with Spanish explorers, starting in 1493. In 1598 a Spanish expedition took horses into New Mexico, along the upper Rio Grande.
In 1680, the Pueblo peoples rose against Spanish rule and drove the settlers out of New Mexico. Many horses were left behind or traded, and they began to spread northward across the Plains.

The Comanche were once part of the Shoshone, a people who lived in the mountains and dry lands to the northwest of the Plains. They spoke the same language family, and they hunted deer, elk and small game.
The future Comanche acquired horses and learned to ride them quickly. A horse could carry a person far faster than walking, and it could pull a load many times heavier than a dog.
In their own language, the Comanche call themselves Numunu, which means the People. The name Comanche comes from the Ute language, and it is often translated as enemy.
In the early 1700s, the Comanche moved south from the mountains onto the southern Plains. The area, known as Comancheria, covered large parts of present-day Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas and New Mexico.
Comanche children were put on ponies as small children and soon rode with great confidence. By their teens, boys and girls could ride all day and look after their own horses.
For the Comanche, wealth meant owning a great many horses. Some families owned dozens, and a few owned hundreds, which they lent, traded or gave as gifts to show their generosity.
A Comanche warrior carried a short bow, which was easy to use on horseback, and often a long lance. His round shield was made of thick buffalo hide and could turn aside an arrow.

Comanche riders were famous for their tricks, such as hanging along the side of a galloping horse. From that position they could shoot arrows from beneath the horse's neck, using the animal as a shield.
On horseback, hunters could ride right alongside a bison and use a lance or a bow at close range. A hunt that once needed a trap now needed only a good horse and a steady hand.
The bison gave the Comanche meat to eat, hides for clothing and tipis, and bones for tools. Even its dried dung was used as fuel, and its tendons were made into strong thread and bowstrings.
A tipi was a cone-shaped tent of buffalo hides stretched over long poles. It was warm in winter and cool in summer, and women could take it down and pack it onto a horse in a short time.
The Comanche were never a single tribe under one ruler. They lived in a number of independent bands, such as the Penateka, the Nokoni and the Quahadi, which each followed their own herds.
A Comanche leader had no power to force anyone to obey. Respect had to be earned by wisdom, bravery and generosity, and big decisions were discussed in councils where many voices could speak.
A young man earned respect by showing courage, skill and generosity. Raids to take horses from enemies were a common way to prove himself, but they could also bring danger and grief.
When the Comanche reached the southern Plains, Apache groups were already living there. After years of war, the Comanche drove them south and west, and took control of the best hunting lands.
The Comanche were skilled traders as well as warriors. They sold hides, meat and horses to farming towns, such as the Wichita villages and Taos, and bought corn, cloth and metal tools.

Traders from New Mexico, known as Comancheros, travelled out onto the dry Plains with carts of bread, corn, cloth and tools. They bought buffalo robes, horses and cattle, and the trade lasted for well over a century.
By the 1780s, the Spanish in New Mexico were tired of Comanche raids. In 1786 the governor, Juan Bautista de Anza, agreed on a peace with Comanche leaders, and it mostly held for many years.
Around 1790, the Comanche made a lasting peace with the Kiowa, another Plains people. From then on the two nations often camped, hunted and fought together.

By about 1800, Comancheria spread over hundreds of thousands of square miles, from the Arkansas River in the north to the Rio Grande in the south. This homeland was larger than many countries in Europe, and the Comanche knew it well.

Some historians call the Comanche world an empire, because other peoples had to deal with its power. Others disagree, because the Comanche had no emperor, no army in the usual sense and no permanent capital.
Disease was a powerful enemy that no horse could outrun. Epidemics of smallpox and cholera, which had come from Europe, killed thousands of Comanche in the 1800s.

After Mexico became independent in 1821, its northern states could not defend themselves. Comanche raiders rode hundreds of miles south and took horses, mules and cattle, which caused great suffering.
In the 1820s and 1830s, settlers from the United States began to move into Texas, which first belonged to Mexico. They built farms on land that the Comanche and others used for hunting.
In March 1840, Comanche leaders came to San Antonio to talk about peace with the Texans. The meeting turned into a violent fight, and more than thirty Comanche, including many leaders, were killed.
In August 1840, hundreds of Comanche warriors rode hundreds of miles to the Gulf coast and raided the town of Linnville. On the way home, Texan fighters stopped them at Plum Creek.

A new weapon appeared in the 1840s, the revolver, which could fire six shots without reloading. Mounted Texas Rangers used it against the Comanche, whose bows and single-shot guns had been the faster weapons until then.

In 1849, the California gold rush sent tens of thousands of travellers across the Plains. They brought cholera, which killed many Comanche, and their wagons frightened the buffalo away from the trails.
In 1867, some Comanche leaders met American officials at Medicine Lodge in Kansas. They agreed to live on a reservation, and in return the United States promised food, supplies and hunting rights.
As railways crossed the Plains, professional hunters arrived to kill buffalo for their hides. Factories bought the leather, and trains carried it east in enormous loads.
By the end of the 1870s, the great southern herd had been killed. The Comanche had lost their main source of food, clothing and shelter, and the old way of life could not continue.
In June 1874, several hundred warriors from the Comanche, Kiowa and Cheyenne attacked a camp of buffalo hunters at Adobe Walls, in Texas. A few dozen men with powerful rifles drove them off.
After Adobe Walls, the United States Army sent several columns of soldiers into the southern Plains. This campaign is called the Red River War, and it lasted from 1874 into 1875.
In September 1874, Colonel Ranald Mackenzie's soldiers surprised a camp in Palo Duro Canyon in Texas. They captured more than a thousand horses and shot most of them, which was a terrible loss.
Hungry and without horses, the Comanche bands came in to the forts one by one. The Quahadi, the last free band, surrendered at Fort Sill in Indian Territory in June 1875.

Life on the reservation was very different from life on the Plains. The Comanche received rations of beef and flour, and many tried to farm, while some earned money by renting grazing land to ranchers.
Many Comanche children were sent to boarding schools run by the government. They had their hair cut, wore uniforms and were forbidden to speak their own language, which caused deep and lasting pain.

In 1901, the reservation was divided into small farms for each family, and the rest was opened to white settlers. In 1903, the Supreme Court said that Congress could change the old treaties without asking.
Even in the hardest years, the Comanche kept their songs, dances and stories alive. They also passed on their history by telling it aloud, which is why oral history is so important today.

In the Second World War, a group of Comanche soldiers used their own language to send secret messages by radio. The enemy could not understand it, and it helped the army, including during the Normandy landings in 1944.

Today the Comanche Nation has its headquarters in Lawton, Oklahoma, and more than 15,000 enrolled members. Very few elders still speak the language fluently, so classes and recordings are helping to keep it alive.

By about 1890, only a few hundred wild bison were left. Thanks to ranchers, conservationists and Native nations, there are now hundreds of thousands in North America, though few of them are truly wild.

The Comanche rose because they learned fast, adapted to new tools and built strong ties through trade. Their story also reminds us to read history from many sides, and to listen to the people it describes.
C1C2: In the heart of North America stretches the Great Plains, an ocean of grass so wide that a traveller could walk for weeks and see little but the horizon. The wind runs across it without anything to stop it, and the summers are hot and the winters bitterly cold. For thousands of years, this open country has been the home of great herds and of the people who followed them.

The animal that dominated the Plains was the American bison, a shaggy, humped giant that weighed as much as a small car and travelled in herds of staggering size. Some historians believe that tens of millions of them once roamed the grasslands, from Canada to Texas. Nothing else supplied so much food, clothing and shelter, and nothing shaped the lives of the Plains peoples so deeply.

For a very long time, the people of the Plains had no animal bigger than a dog to carry their goods, so they walked, and the dogs dragged small loads on frames of poles called travois. Camps moved only a short distance each day, and no family could own more than a few possessions. The reach of every hunter ended at the point where his own tired legs gave out, and the herds simply moved on without him.

A hunter on foot who tried to approach a bison risked being trampled, so the people of the Plains relied on patience, cooperation and cunning. In some places, large groups guided a herd towards a cliff or a pen and killed the animals as they fell or became trapped. It could feed a community for months, but it depended on luck, season and the position of the herd.

Strangely, the horse is a native of North America, for its earliest ancestors evolved on this continent over millions of years before spreading to other lands. At the end of the last ice age, about 10,000 years ago, wild horses vanished from the Americas, and scientists still argue about the reasons. For thousands of years afterwards, there was not a single horse here for anyone to ride.

The horse came back with Spanish ships in 1493, carried to the islands of the Caribbean by sailors who valued it as a weapon and a mount. In 1598, a Spanish expedition took herds of horses north into New Mexico, where it set up settlements among the Pueblo peoples. The newcomers tried to keep horses away from the native people, but they could not control them for long.

The Spanish settlers in New Mexico forced the Pueblo people to labour and tried to suppress their religion, and in 1680 the Pueblo villages rose together against them in a great revolt. The Spanish were driven south for more than a decade, leaving horses and equipment behind. Through trade, gifts and raids, those animals passed from hand to hand and began to spread across the Plains.

The ancestors of the Comanche belonged to the Shoshone, who lived in the mountains and the dry basins of what is now the western United States. They spoke closely related languages and lived in small family groups, hunting small game and gathering roots and seeds. Sometime in the 1600s, a group of them began to drift towards the grassland, drawn by the herds and by the animals from the south.

Having acquired horses, the people who would become the Comanche discovered an entirely new scale of life, since one animal could carry a rider faster and farther than any hunter had dreamed. A horse could drag a load many times heavier than a dog, and it gave its owner a view over the grass that no walker could have. Within a couple of generations, almost everything about their daily life had been transformed.

In their own language, the Comanche have always called themselves Numunu, a word that simply means the People. The name by which the world knows them was borrowed from the Ute, a neighbouring nation, and it is often translated as enemy or as someone who wants to fight all the time. It tells us how others saw them, but it is not the whole of who they were.

By the early 1700s, the Comanche had pushed south and east out of the mountains onto the grasslands, where the herds were thickest and the horses were within reach. They gradually claimed an enormous territory that later became known as Comancheria, covering large parts of what are now Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, New Mexico and Colorado. It was not a country with fixed borders, but a living network of hunting grounds, trade routes and camps.

Children grew up on horseback, and many were riding ponies alone before they were old enough to be given real work. By the time a boy reached his teens, he could stay in the saddle for a whole day, handle a half-wild animal and care for it like a friend. The result was a standard of horsemanship that astonished the Spanish, the Mexicans and the Americans alike.

Among the Comanche, a man's wealth was measured not by gold or land but by the size of his herd, and a few families owned hundreds of animals. Horses were traded, lent, stolen and given away, and a leader who gave generously gained respect that no amount of money could buy. Caring for such large herds also required skill, grass and water, and a constant watch for thieves.

The favourite weapon of the Comanche was a short, powerful bow made of tough wood and strengthened with animal sinew, which a rider could fire easily from the saddle. Many warriors also carried a long lance and a round shield of thick buffalo hide that could turn aside arrows and, sometimes, even a bullet. When guns became common, they were added to the arsenal rather than replacing the older weapons.

Observers of every nation described the Comanche as the finest horsemen on the continent, and the feats they reported seem almost unbelievable. A rider could slip down the side of his galloping horse, hooking a heel over its back, and fire arrow after arrow from beneath its neck. Attackers who struck in swift, scattered groups, instead of marching in rows, confused many armies that were trained in a different way.

Riding beside the herds, a mounted hunter could select an animal, close the distance and kill it with a single lance thrust or a well-aimed arrow. A good buffalo horse learned to run close to the huge beasts without flinching, and it was prized above almost every other possession. The hunts were still dangerous, but they brought home more food than anyone had ever dreamed of.

Almost nothing from a bison went to waste, for the meat was eaten fresh or dried, the hides became tipis, robes and moccasins, and the bones were shaped into tools. Sinew provided thread and bowstrings, the horns became cups and spoons, and dry dung fed the fires on a land with few trees. Much of this work was carried out by women, whose skill with a hide was the foundation of the household.

The home of a Comanche family was the tipi, a cone of buffalo hides wrapped around a frame of long poles, with a smoke hole at the top and a fire in the middle. Women owned and managed it, and with practice they could pitch or strike one in surprisingly little time. This portable house, together with horses to carry it, allowed the whole camp to follow the herds across the seasons.

There was never a single Comanche state with a government and a capital, and no ruler spoke for everyone. Instead, the people lived in a number of independent bands, among them the Penateka, Kotsoteka, Yamparika, Nokoni and Quahadi, and each followed its own pattern of hunting and trading. Bands might gather for a summer festival or an important decision, but they were just as likely to drift apart again.

Comanche leaders could not command, because the whole culture rested on individual freedom, and a man was followed only for as long as people trusted his judgement. A band might have one respected leader for peace and another for war, and decisions were reached by long discussion in a council. The system was flexible, but it also meant that no single leader could speak for the whole people.

For young Comanche men, reputation was everything, and it was won by courage, by skill with a horse and by giving freely to others. Raids against enemy camps, to capture horses or to avenge a loss, were the usual way of proving that courage, and some were rewarded with songs and status. Such raids also brought suffering to many families, whose own children and animals were sometimes the victims.

The southern Plains were not empty when the Comanche arrived, since Apache groups had lived there for generations, hunting and farming along the rivers. In the first half of the 1700s, a long series of wars forced the Apache southwards and westwards, and the Comanche took over the herds and the grass. The conflict was long and bitter, and it created enmities that were still alive in the memory of both peoples many generations later.

Far from being merely raiders, the Comanche became the great merchants of the southern Plains, supplying hides, meat and horses to farming peoples who lacked them. At the annual fairs of Taos and in the Wichita and Taovayas villages on the Red River, they swapped these goods for corn, tobacco, cloth and metal tools. Their power, in other words, came as much from the market as it ever did from the battlefield, and visitors who wished to trade had to respect it.

Traders from the Spanish-speaking villages of New Mexico, called Comancheros, drove their creaking carts far out onto the dry Staked Plains to meet the Comanche camps. They brought bread, corn, cloth and iron, and went home with buffalo robes, horses and cattle, some of which had been taken in raids elsewhere. The trade flourished for well over a hundred years, and neither the Spanish nor the Americans could stop it.

Spanish officials in New Mexico spent much of the 1700s alternately fighting the Comanche and paying for peace, and neither policy brought lasting calm. In 1786, Governor Juan Bautista de Anza negotiated a treaty with Comanche leaders that included trade, gifts and cooperation against the Apache. The peace was far from perfect, as raids and misunderstandings continued, but it mostly held for about a generation.

Around 1790, the Comanche settled their old quarrel with the Kiowa, a Plains people who had come from the north, and the two nations became close allies. They shared hunting grounds, joined forces against common enemies and often camped side by side. The friendship, which lasted into the reservation years and beyond, helped to make the southern Plains harder for outsiders to enter.

At its height, around the start of the nineteenth century, the territory the Comanche dominated stretched across hundreds of thousands of square miles, from the Arkansas River in the north to central Texas and the borders of northern Mexico. It was larger than many European countries, and its people knew every spring and canyon of it. No outside power could cross it, build in it or trade within it without their consent.

Some modern historians describe this system as a Comanche empire, because other peoples paid tribute, sought permission to trade and adjusted their lives around Comanche power. Others object that the word suggests a government with a capital and a bureaucracy, which the Comanche never had. The debate is useful, however, since it forces us to ask what power really means and how we ought to recognise it in a society so different from our own.

The deadliest enemy of the Comanche was neither a rival nation nor an army but disease, because they had no protection against illnesses that came from Europe. Repeated outbreaks of smallpox and cholera in the 1800s killed thousands of people, and some historians think the population fell sharply from perhaps 20,000 or more around 1800. Each epidemic weakened the bands, and the losses came at the very moment when new and more powerful enemies were approaching.

After Mexico won its independence from Spain in 1821, the government in the capital had little power to protect its distant northern states. In the 1830s and 1840s, Comanche war parties rode far into the interior, driving off horses, mules and cattle and sometimes taking captives. The raids caused immense suffering in border towns, and some villages were abandoned altogether.

Families from the United States began to move into Texas during the 1820s, first as settlers invited by Mexico and later as citizens of an independent Republic of Texas. They fenced farms, felled timber and built towns on land that had been hunting ground for generations. Conflict was almost inevitable, because both peoples believed the land was theirs, and neither side was willing to give way.

In March 1840, a group of Comanche leaders rode into San Antonio to negotiate a treaty with the Texans, bringing women and children with them. The talks collapsed when the Texans tried to hold the chiefs as hostages, and in the confusion more than thirty Comanche, many of them leaders, were killed. The Comanche viewed the event as a terrible betrayal, and it was not forgotten.

In August 1840, several hundred Comanche warriors rode hundreds of miles across Texas to the Gulf coast, plundering the town of Linnville as its people fled to ships. On their way home, laden with goods and horses, they were intercepted at Plum Creek by Texans, and much of their plunder was lost. The raid showed both the reach of Comanche power and the limits of it.

In the 1840s, the invention of the Colt revolver gave mounted Texans a weapon they had never had before, a pistol that could fire repeatedly without reloading. Until then, a Comanche with a bow could shoot several arrows in the time a settler needed to reload a rifle, which had been a great advantage in battle. The revolver changed that balance, and Texas Rangers learned to use it with deadly effect.

When gold was found in California in 1849, tens of thousands of fortune hunters poured westward along trails that crossed the Plains. They brought cholera with them, and the disease ravaged the Comanche that year, while their animals, wagons and campfires scared the buffalo and ate the grass. The old balance of the Plains was being overturned, quietly at first and then with growing speed, by people who had no idea what they were doing.

In October 1867, representatives of the United States met leaders of the Comanche, Kiowa and Kiowa-Apache at Medicine Lodge Creek in Kansas, and the treaty they signed promised a reservation in what is now Oklahoma. In return, the Americans promised food, goods and the right to hunt buffalo south of the Arkansas River. Not all the Comanche bands agreed to the terms, and in practice the promises were poorly kept.

Once railways reached the Plains, professional hunters arrived in their thousands, killing bison for hides that factories in the East turned into leather belts, shoes and coats. Trains carried the hides eastward in enormous loads, and the hunters, with their long-range rifles, could shoot hundreds of animals in a day. Some officials even welcomed the slaughter, because they knew the Plains peoples could not live without the herds.

Within a few terrible years, the great southern herd was reduced to bones that lay bleaching across the grass, and the main source of food, shelter and clothing of the Comanche had disappeared. By around 1890, only a few hundred wild bison were left in the entire country. Without them, the economy that had supported the Comanche for a century and a half collapsed.

In June 1874, several hundred warriors from the Comanche, Kiowa and Cheyenne attacked the hide hunters' camp at Adobe Walls in the Texas Panhandle, hoping to stop the slaughter of the herds. The few dozen hunters inside the buildings used powerful long-range rifles to hold them off. The failure was a heavy blow to the confidence of the Plains peoples, and it did nothing at all to stop the slaughter that had caused the attack.

After Adobe Walls, the United States Army decided to end the problem for good, and it sent five columns of cavalry and infantry converging on the southern Plains. The campaign, known as the Red River War, was fought through a bitterly hot summer and a freezing winter. The soldiers did not just fight warriors but also hunted for camps, food and animals.

In September 1874, Colonel Ranald Mackenzie's soldiers found a big camp in the hidden depths of Palo Duro Canyon in Texas and attacked it at dawn. The people escaped on foot, but the soldiers seized more than a thousand horses and shot most of them. For a horse people, nothing could have been more devastating, because without their herds they could neither hunt nor travel.

Starving, cold and stripped of their horses, one band after another came in to the army forts to surrender. The Quahadi, who had lived free on the high Staked Plains longer than any other group, reached Fort Sill in what is now Oklahoma in June 1875. The independent Comanche way of life, and the age of the horse on the southern Plains, had come to an end.

The reservation in southwestern Oklahoma brought a new and humbling life, with rations of beef and flour handed out by officials and agents. Some families tried farming on dry, difficult soil, while leaders negotiated leases with Texan cattle ranchers who paid to graze their herds on the reservation grass. It was a pale reflection of the old freedom, but people worked hard to hold their families together.

To change the habits of the next generation, the government sent Comanche children to boarding schools, where they were given new clothes and new names and had their hair cut. They were punished for speaking their own language, and many fell ill or were homesick for years at a time. The policy aimed to erase a culture, and it caused wounds that families still remember.

At the start of the twentieth century, the reservation was divided into small plots for individual families, and the surplus land was opened to settlers in 1901 through a lottery. A Kiowa leader, Lone Wolf, took the case to court, and in 1903 the Supreme Court ruled that Congress could change Native treaties on its own authority. The decision left tribes with far less legal protection than they had hoped for.

Despite the pressures of the reservation years, the Comanche preserved their ceremonies, songs and family ties, and gatherings with dances and drumming continued into the twentieth century. The elders passed their history down by telling it aloud, and those spoken memories are now treated as valuable evidence alongside Spanish letters, army reports and the diaries of travellers. Culture, it turned out, could survive even when the old way of life had gone.

In the Second World War, a small group of Comanche soldiers were selected to send secret radio messages in their own language, which almost nobody outside their nation understood. They helped the American army in Europe, including during the Normandy landings of 1944, and the enemy never cracked their code. The language that the schools had tried to silence became a weapon that helped to save lives.

Today the Comanche Nation governs itself from its headquarters in Lawton, Oklahoma, with more than 15,000 enrolled citizens who live both near the old reservation and in cities across the country. Very few elders still speak the Comanche language fluently, and teachers are now working with recordings, classes and young people to bring it back. The People are still here, and they are writing the next chapter of their own history for themselves, in their own words.

The bison came terrifyingly close to extinction, and after the slaughter only a few hundred wild animals remained by around 1890. A handful of ranchers, conservationists and Native peoples then protected the survivors, and today hundreds of thousands live in North America, although only a small fraction roam free. Many tribes now manage their own herds, partly to restore the animal and partly to restore a relationship that was broken.

The Comanche rose to power because they combined a new animal with old knowledge, flexible leadership and a talent for trade, and they fell because of disease, shifting borders and the loss of the herds. A fair account must therefore listen to Spanish, Mexican, American and Comanche voices alike, and it must admit the suffering on every side. Understanding history in this way is harder than telling a legend, but it is far more honest.
